newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA bomb kills one in Spain, dampens peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: ETA bomb kills one in Spain, dampens peace hopes.

text.p: A huge car bomb blast in southern Spain killed a serviceman on Monday and Officials said it dampened hopes for negotiated peace with the Basque separatist group ETA, which they blamed for the attack.
The car bomb, which injured seven other people, three seriously, exploded at 7.15 a.m. (0615 GMT) about two km (one mile) outside Granada's city centre near a military airbase.
The blast destroyed a passing military van, broke windows in a wide area and heavily damaged a nearby apartment building.
Police said the attackers probably set it off by remote control from a dark car seen speeding away from the scene.

The attack followed a weekend of turbulent support for ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), which has killed some 800 people in its 29-year drive for Basque independence. Officials said it effectively chilled any move toward talks with the rebels.
"It's very difficult at times like these today that anyone could even bring this topic up," Spain's Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja told state radio from Jerusalem.
The minister cut short an official visit to Israel, where he was to talk about fighting urban guerrillas and organised crime, and returned to Spain to visit the victims and their families.

The death of the serviceman, a barber, is the third this year that the government has blamed on ETA. The other two were point-blank shootings, killing an army officer in Madrid on January 8 and a bicycle vendor in San Sebastian on January 30.
Despite the ferocity of its recent activity, ETA has enjoyed renewed support among Basques in the past six months.

Groups of hooded youths affiliated with the rebels regularly rampage through Basque towns and cities on weekend nights firebombing public property, smashing windows and spray painting pro-ETA slogans.
Last weekend, dozens of people were injured and property was damaged in protests and demonstrations in the northern region after an alleged ETA prisoner was found hanged in his cell.
An autopsy report said the prisoner had been depressed for several weeks and had killed himself, but hundreds of Basques took to the streets arguing it was murder.
Prison officials later confirmed a report in the radical Basque daily Egin that his feet and hands were tied at the time of his death, but they insisted he had committed suicide.
Members of the Herri Batasuna (HB) party, which does not rule out violence as a means to achieve independence, called on Saturday for demonstrations and strikes to protest over the jailings.
Five HB leaders were sent to prison last week for refusing to appear in Spain's Supreme Court to answer charges they promoted violence.
On Sunday, some 2,000 people attended the prisoner's funeral chanting "Long live ETA" in support of HB and against more moderate Basque politicians.
